  • Official MeshCore source and releases

docs.title: MeshCore questions and answers
docs.text:
Search this page with your browser's Find command, or choose a topic below. Settings can differ by place, so this page links to the current source instead of repeating values that may change.

  • Settings and range
  • Hardware
  • Joining or starting a mesh
  • Observers and troubleshooting

docs.title: Which radio settings should I use in Canada?
docs.text:
Use the radio profile in the community directory. If none is published, choose Canada in the app for the Canadian radio settings and 3-byte paths. See the preset details and older-app guidance.

The separate USA preset uses the same radio values but leaves the path-hash setting unchanged. Upstream preset update.

The repeater configurator selects IATA regions and generates independent scope commands. Its radio and advert ID controls remain separate and keep current settings until you choose a change.

docs.title: What is path hash mode?
docs.text:
Paths record short repeater identifiers of 1, 2, or 3 bytes. On a repeater, path.hash.mode controls its own adverts; it does not restrict the path-hash sizes it can forward. A companion’s setting controls the path size of its outgoing messages.

MeshCore Canada recommends 3-byte paths. Repeaters on firmware 1.14 or newer can forward all three sizes; older repeaters drop packets using 2- or 3-byte paths. Follow your community’s settings while older repeaters are being upgraded. See the upstream multibyte FAQ.

Read the region standard.

docs.title: Do I need an amateur radio licence?
docs.text:
MeshCore Canada cannot decide which authorization applies to your station. You are responsible for legal frequency, power, antenna, and operating choices in your location.

Start with the Canadian regulatory links. If you are unsure, ask a qualified local operator before transmitting.

docs.title: What range should I expect?
docs.text: Range depends on antenna quality and placement, height, terrain, buildings, interference, and line of sight. Test against a nearby known-good node before assuming the device or firmware is faulty.

docs.title: Which devices work with MeshCore?
docs.text:
Use a device listed by the official MeshCore Flasher or by a MeshCore Canada guide for the role you need. Support depends on the board and firmware target.

Compare device roles, then open the hardware guide from the matching setup guide.

docs.title: Can I reuse a device that currently runs Meshtastic?
docs.text:
Some supported boards can be reflashed with MeshCore firmware. A device still running Meshtastic firmware will not join a MeshCore network.

Confirm the exact board in the official flasher before changing it, and back up anything you need to keep.

docs.title: Which board should I buy first?
docs.text: Choose the role first. For a companion, prefer a supported device with nearby community experience. For a fixed service, reliable power, antenna placement, and maintainability matter more than screen features.

docs.title: How do I join a nearby mesh?
docs.text:
1. Find the local community.
  2. Follow its published settings or use the Canadian baseline when no override is listed.
  3. Follow the setup guide for your device role.
  4. Send an advert and ask a nearby user to confirm it.

docs.title: How do I start a mesh where none is listed?
docs.text:
Begin with companions so people can test locally. Add fixed infrastructure only after checking placement, power, local coordination, and the region standard.

When the group is ready, add the community so others can find its status, contact information, and any reviewed local settings.

docs.title: Why does my observer show no packets?
docs.text:
A connection to the data service does not prove the radio is hearing nearby traffic. Check the selected radio settings, packet publishing, device activity, and the final verification result.

Use Check your observer, then follow observer troubleshooting for the symptom you see.

docs.title: Where can I ask another question?
docs.text: Use Get help for the shortest support route. Remove passwords, private keys, precise private locations, and other sensitive values before sharing screenshots or logs.

docs.title: Common tasks in the MeshCore app
docs.text:
Choose a task. The screenshots show one version of the MeshCore mobile app, so labels and positions may differ.

  • Send your first message
  • Share your contact link
  • Import a contact link
  • Trace a path
  • Check heard repeats

Before you start

  • Connect the app to your companion.
  • Confirm the companion can send and receive locally.
  • Do not post private keys, passwords, or precise private locations in a shared screenshot.

docs.title: Send your first message
docs.text:
1. Connect the app to your companion and confirm the local radio settings.
  2. Open the channel used by your community, or choose an imported contact.
  3. Send a short greeting and ask for a reply.

A reply confirms two-way communication. A sent indicator alone does not confirm delivery. If nobody replies, check with a nearby operator before sending more tests.

docs.title: Share your contact link
docs.text:
Use this when another person needs to add you as a contact.

  1. Open the MeshCore app and connect to your companion.

  2. Open the Signal screen.

  3. Select Advert, then To Clipboard.

  4. Paste the contact link into the conversation where you intend to share it.

The clipboard now contains a contact link that another MeshCore user can import.

docs.title: Import a contact link
docs.text:
Use this after another person sends you their MeshCore contact link.

  1. Copy only the contact link, then connect the app to your companion.

  2. Open the three-dot menu.

  3. Select Add Contact.

  4. Select Import from Clipboard Link.

  5. Wait for the success message and the new-contact notice.

The named contact now appears in your contact list.

If the import fails, copy the original link again without extra words or punctuation. Ask the sender for a new link if it still fails.

docs.title: Trace a path
docs.text: A manual trace tests the repeater sequence you select. It does not guarantee that later messages will use the same path.

docs.title: Open the trace tool
docs.text:
1. Connect the app to your companion.

  2. Open the three-dot menu.

  3. Select Tools.

  4. Select Trace Path - Manual.

  5. Select the plus button to add a repeater.

docs.title: Trace one repeater
docs.text:
1. Add one repeater and confirm its identifier.

  2. Select Trace Path.

docs.title: Trace through several repeaters
docs.text:
1. Add the repeaters in the forward order required by the path.

  2. Add the return sequence shown by your local path plan.

  3. Review the complete sequence, then select Trace.

  4. Read the result.

If you do not know the forward and return sequence, ask the local community instead of guessing repeater identifiers.

docs.title: Check heard repeats
docs.text:
A heard repeat means your companion received a repeated copy of a packet it sent. A missing repeat does not by itself show where the packet failed: the repeater may not have heard the packet, or your companion may not have heard the repeated copy.

  1. Send a message in the intended channel.

  2. When Heard n repeats appears below the message, press and hold the message.

  3. Select Heard Repeats.

  4. Review the repeaters your companion heard for that packet.

  5. Select a repeater to inspect the reported path.

docs.title: Need help?
docs.text: If a result is missing or unclear, compare one known-good nearby node and then use Get help. Include the task and step where you stopped, but remove sensitive values before sharing a screenshot.

docs.title: What is MeshCore?
docs.text:
MeshCore is a LoRa mesh network. A device's firmware gives it a specific job.

MeshCore project split, use the official links

Due to recent events in the MeshCore development team, the project has split. To stay on the official track, please only use:

  • Flashing tool and blog: meshcore.io
  • Source code: github.com/meshcore-dev/MeshCore
  • Discord (named "MeshCore.io"): discord.com/invite/fUfWevRXAg

Read more about the split: The Split, blog.meshcore.io.

docs.title: Device roles
docs.text:
• A companion sends and receives messages.
  • A repeater forwards traffic and extends coverage.
  • A room server keeps a shared room available.
  • An observer sends heard network data to CoreScope.

Compare device roles.

docs.title: Settings in Canada
docs.text: Check the community directory before configuring a device. Use its local settings when listed; otherwise use the Canada defaults.

docs.title: Official MeshCore resources
docs.text:
MeshCore Canada covers Canadian communities, settings, and tools. For official firmware, apps, and protocol information, use:

  • MeshCore documentation
  • MeshCore Flasher
  • MeshCore source code

Choose a role and start setup

docs.title: Change a repeater ID in 1-byte mode
docs.text:
Only for legacy 1-byte regions

Canada uses 3-byte path hashes by default. Continue only if your local region operator has confirmed this repeater must stay in 1-byte mode and approved the new ID.

docs.title: What this will change
docs.text: Changing the private key changes the node identity. It can break existing administration, contact, and tracking relationships. The old key is the only identity rollback path.

docs.title: Prerequisites and backup
docs.text:
1. Confirm with the local region operator that the repeater must remain in 1-byte mode and that a new ID is required.
  2. Connect to the repeater and record its current public key with get public.key.
  3. Over a trusted serial connection, back up the current private key with get prv.key and store it as a secret in a secure location.
  4. Confirm the proposed 2–6 character ID is unused in the local region's coordination record.

Never post or transmit either private key through an issue, screenshot, public chat, or log. The saved old private key is the rollback path.

JavaScript is required for the live duplicate-ID check. You can also [open the live node directory](https://live.meshcore.ca/?tab=Nodes).

docs.title: Generate and apply the key
docs.text:
1. Open the MeshCore Key Generator.
  2. Enter the locally approved, unused 2–6 character ID and select Generate Key.
  3. Confirm the generated private key is a 64-character hexadecimal value.
  4. Copy it directly to the trusted repeater console without saving it in an ordinary note or chat.

  5. Run, replacing the placeholder with the generated value:

    set prv.key <PRIVATE-KEY>

  6. Reboot the repeater.

docs.title: Verify and restore
docs.text:
After reboot, run get public.key and confirm its prefix matches the locally approved ID. Recheck admin access, radio settings, region configuration, adverts, and local routing before returning the repeater to service.

If verification fails, restore the backed-up old private key with set prv.key <OLD-PRIVATE-KEY>, reboot, and confirm the original public key and access are restored.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: If admin access, the public-key prefix, adverts, region configuration, or routing is wrong, keep the repeater on the bench. Restore the backed-up old private key over the trusted serial connection, reboot, and confirm the complete former state before returning it to service.

docs.title: Record the change
docs.text: Record the locally approved ID, operator approval, old/new public-key prefixes, verification, and rollback location without recording either private key in the public maintenance record.

docs.title: Verification limits
docs.text: This procedure has not been tested against current firmware. Have the local region operator review it before use.

docs.title: Update a repeater or room server over the air
docs.text:
Use USB when you can. An over-the-air update is a higher-risk fallback for supported nRF52 devices, and a failed update may still need USB recovery. Confirm the exact board, bootloader, installed version, and firmware file before continuing.

Bootloader prerequisite

Proceed only after confirming that the exact board has the OTAFIX bootloader described in Flashing a Repeater. A failed OTA update can require physical USB recovery.

Android is the method tested by the community

The community has observed failed OTA attempts from iOS and currently recommends Android for this workflow. This is a local risk-control recommendation, not a claim that upstream iOS support does not exist.

docs.title: Prerequisites: decide whether to stop
docs.text:
Use USB instead if any answer below is no:

  • [ ] The device is an OTA-supported nRF52 board such as a RAK4631, Heltec T114, or XIAO nRF52840.
  • [ ] The board identity, installed bootloader, current firmware, and intended firmware file are known.
  • [ ] The private key, settings, region configuration, and access details are backed up securely.
  • [ ] Stable power and a reliable radio-management path are available for the full update.
  • [ ] Someone can reach the device with a USB cable if OTA fails.
  • [ ] The downloaded ZIP names the exact board and role.

No physical recovery means no OTA

Do not start an OTA update on a roof, tower, winter site, or other inaccessible installation when a failed update cannot be recovered promptly by USB.

docs.title: What the update changes
docs.text: OTA places the device into firmware-update mode and replaces its firmware over Bluetooth. A failed transfer can leave the device needing physical USB recovery, while a wrong artifact can target the wrong board or role.

docs.title: Recovery plan before starting
docs.text: Keep the correct USB firmware and a data cable ready. Record the current version and settings. If the device remains in DFU mode after a failed attempt, scan again for a generic DFU name and retry the same verified ZIP. If it does not recover over the air, stop and reflash the exact board/role by USB using the backup.

docs.title: 1. Download the Exact Firmware ZIP
docs.text:
1. Open the MeshCore Web Flasher.
  2. Select the exact device and Repeater or Room Server role.
  3. Choose the specific version approved for this update; do not rely on a generic “latest” label.
  4. Use the download control to save the .zip artifact.

Alternatively, use the official MeshCore releases and verify the artifact is for the exact board and role.

docs.title: 2. Put the Device in OTA Mode
docs.text:
1. In the MeshCore mobile app, log in with the admin password.

  2. Open Command Line and run:

    start ota

  3. Continue only after a reply similar to OK - mac: FF:AA:BB ... confirms OTA mode. If there is no confirmation, stop and keep the device on its current firmware.

You may also issue start ota from a standalone management device that supports the repeater command line.

docs.title: 3. Transfer the Update
docs.text:
Install Nordic's nRF Device Firmware Update app from the official app store for the phone.

For the Android method tested by the community, use:

  • Packet receipts notification: on
  • Number of packets: 8
  • Request high MTU: off
  • Disable resume: on
  • Prepare object delay: 0 ms
  • Force scanning: on

Then:

  1. Select the verified .zip file.
  2. Select the expected device from the scan list.
  3. Start the update and keep the phone, device, and power stable until the app reports completion.

If the app reports failure but a generic name such as AdaDFU or RAK4631_DFU appears, select that device and retry the same verified ZIP once. Do not switch to another board's file.

docs.title: Check the transfer
docs.text: The DFU app reports completion, the device restarts, remote administration reconnects, and the device reports the intended firmware version. Anything less is a failed or incomplete update.

docs.title: 4. Test the update
docs.text:
1. Log out and reconnect after the device restarts.
  2. Run ver and confirm the exact intended firmware version.
  3. Run clock; if needed, run clock sync from a supported remote management device.
  4. Confirm the radio, path-hash, region, advert, access, and role settings still match the saved configuration.
  5. Send an advert and complete a local message-routing test.

The update is not complete until the device reconnects, reports the intended version, retains its configuration, and passes the local test.

For upstream context, see the official MeshCore OTA instructions.

docs.title: Recovery after a failed update
docs.text: If the same verified ZIP cannot complete against the expected DFU device, stop remote attempts and recover the exact board/role by USB. Restore the backed-up identity and settings where supported, then repeat the complete verification. Never try a different board artifact as a recovery guess.

docs.title: After the update
docs.text: Record the old and new versions, artifact filename/source, device identity, result, settings check, radio test, and recovery status in the repeater maintenance record.

docs.title: What has been tested
docs.text: The Android recommendation and DFU settings come from community testing. They are not a complete test matrix for every board, firmware version, phone, or app.

docs.title: Canada defaults
docs.text:
Use these settings unless your local community lists different ones.

Setting Canada default Radio preset Canada Raw radio values 910.525 MHz / 62.5 kHz / SF7 / CR5 Path hash mode 3-byte Command-line path setting set path.hash.mode 2

The MeshCore app now has separate Canada and USA presets. Both use the radio values above, but Canada also selects 3-byte paths. USA leaves the path-hash setting unchanged. You can still change that setting manually. See the September 9 preset update.

If your app or flasher still shows USA/Canada (Recommended), use it for the same radio values and set 3-byte paths separately. Update repeaters older than firmware 1.14 before relying on multi-byte paths; those older versions cannot forward them.

Check local settings first

Nearby devices need matching settings. A card marked Different local settings takes precedence over the Canada defaults after you confirm it with the listed community.

docs.title: MeshCore glossary
docs.text: Use your browser's Find command to jump to a term. Definitions are short; the linked guides explain how to use each setting or device.

docs.title: A-D
docs.text: Advert A MeshCore announcement packet that helps nearby nodes learn about a device and its path. Bandwidth A LoRa radio setting that affects how much radio spectrum a transmission uses. Use the value from your local settings or the configurator. Broker A service that receives and distributes messages for Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT). Coding rate (CR) A LoRa error-correction setting. Use the value from your local settings or the configurator. Companion A personal MeshCore device used to send and receive messages. It often connects to an app and does not relay mesh traffic. CoreScope MeshCore Canada's public tools for viewing observers, packets, nodes, and map data.

docs.title: F-M
docs.text: Firmware Software installed on a device. MeshCore firmware is built for a specific board and role. Industrial, scientific, and medical (ISM) band Radio spectrum used by many low-power devices. Legal use still depends on location, equipment, and operating conditions. JSON Web Token (JWT) A time-limited credential used by supported MeshCore Canada data services. Treat it as sensitive. Location code A short code that groups observer data by area. Some observer guides call this an IATA code because they use three-letter airport codes. LoRa The long-range, low-power radio modulation used by MeshCore devices. Mesh network A network in which supported devices can relay traffic instead of relying on one central radio. Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) A publish-and-subscribe protocol used by observers to send network data to public tools.

docs.title: N-R
docs.text: Node Any MeshCore device on the network. Observer A radio or host service that listens for MeshCore traffic and sends network data to public tools. Observing and repeating are separate functions; a node can do both when configured for it. Path hash mode The MeshCore setting that controls the size of identifiers in advert paths. Use the value from the current local or Canadian configuration. Preset A named group of radio settings. Repeater A normally fixed MeshCore device that relays packets to extend network coverage. Room server A MeshCore device that keeps a shared room available to companions. Its main job is hosting the room, not extending coverage.

docs.title: S-W
docs.text: Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) A measurement comparing a received signal with background noise. Spreading factor (SF) A LoRa setting that affects airtime, data rate, and reception. Use the value from your local settings or the configurator. WebSocket A long-lived web connection. Some MQTT clients use WebSockets to reach a broker through normal web network paths.

docs.title: Start with MeshCore
docs.text:
Pick the guide that matches what you want the device to do:

  • Send and receive messages with a companion.
  • Improve local coverage with a repeater.
  • Host a persistent room with a room server.
  • Share data with CoreScope with an observer.

Not sure which one fits? Compare the roles.

docs.title: Before setup
docs.text: Check the community directory for local radio settings. If none are listed, use the Canada defaults. Each setup guide covers preparation, configuration, and a quick working check.

docs.title: Choose a MeshCore role
docs.text:
Choose a role based on the job the device will do.

Role Use it for Relays mesh traffic? Usually Setup Companion Send and receive messages Normally no Mobile; often pairs with a phone Set up a companion Repeater Improve local coverage Yes Fixed with continuous power Set up a repeater Room server Keep a shared room available Can, but not recommended Fixed with continuous power Set up a room server Observer Send heard network data to CoreScope No Fixed; requirements vary Set up an observer

docs.title: Role details
docs.text:
Companion nodes are the small personal devices (handheld or portable) that let a user connect to the mesh.

  • Run on battery or USB power.
  • Usually pair with a smartphone over Bluetooth for messaging.
  • Standalone options like the T-Deck include a screen and keyboard, but we don't recommend them for beginners since the firmware is still rough.
  • Normally do not route packets. Client repeat is a limited off-grid feature; leave it off on an established public mesh unless local guidance says otherwise.

Repeaters are fixed installations, typically mounted at elevation (rooftop, tower, mast), that extend range and link mesh segments.

  • Run continuously on mains or solar power. Most Ottawa repeaters operate on solar.
  • Form the recommended routing backbone for an established mesh.

Room servers run specialized firmware that functions like a persistent chat room or mini-BBS.

  • When a companion connects, it can retrieve up to 32 unseen messages, similar to checking an inbox.
  • Can repeat, but this is not recommended. Ottawa keeps repeat disabled on room servers and uses separate repeaters.
  • Lack several repeater and remote-administration features. Use them as shared message rooms, not as network repeaters.

New to MeshCore? Start with a companion. Before buying or flashing, confirm that the setup guide supports your device.

If none of these roles fits, ask the community before buying hardware.

docs.title: Start with a companion
docs.text:
A companion is a personal messaging device. It does not route traffic for other users. Most pair with an app; some have their own screen and controls.

Install and configure a companion

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Check the recommended companion options.
  • Confirm the detailed flashing guide lists your device.
  • Use a data-capable USB cable and a supported browser.
  • Record any identity or settings you need before following an erase step.

docs.title: Know what flashing changes
docs.text: The linked flashing guide replaces the device firmware and configures it as a companion. Stop before erasing if you cannot recover information you need.

docs.title: Flash the companion
docs.text: Follow Flash and configure a companion.

docs.title: Use the right radio settings
docs.text:
Use Canada with the 3-byte path setting unless your community lists different settings.

If Canada is not listed, follow the older-preset instructions.

Match your local mesh

Check the community directory. If your community publishes different settings, use those settings instead.

Reboot after changing the radio settings, then send an advert.

docs.title: Choose a scope
docs.text:
ON/QC: wait for Phase 2

For personal companions, leave Default Region Scope empty and channels unscoped for now. Phase 2 is not open. It can start no earlier than January 2027, after the repeaters are ready and the rollout is announced. Switching early can prevent your messages from reaching other users.

Find your city code on the IATA region map. When Phase 2 is announced, use onqc for your default scope and Public channel, and your city scope, such as yow, for test channels. Leave can and na for future use.

Bot and MeshMapper operators follow the end-of-Phase-1 instructions, once local repeaters are ready. See the rollout order before changing scopes.

Elsewhere, use the scope agreed by your local community. See the scope setup guide for app requirements and examples. Scopes do not change your radio settings.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
The companion is ready when:

  1. the device shows the Canada settings or your community's settings; and
  2. a nearby known-good device or community member can see its advert.

Use the companion verification checklist.

docs.title: Setup checklist
docs.text:
Checks are saved only in this browser.

  1. Confirm compatible hardware
  2. Back up and prepare
  3. Follow the flashing guide
  4. Apply Canada or local settings
  5. Check the device nearby
  6. Test with another mesh user

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Keep the local settings recorded and check them again after firmware changes. Use MeshCore how-to guides for common messaging tasks. Find your community, then exchange a test message with a nearby user. If nobody can see the advert, get help.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
Start with the symptom. Do not post passwords, private keys, precise locations, or unredacted command output.

What is wrong? Start here You are unsure which role or hardware fits Compare roles A nearby device cannot see your advert Recheck the verification steps and local settings You need local settings or another person to test Find a community An observer is missing or has no recent activity Observer troubleshooting You need a common MeshCore answer MeshCore FAQ A page is missing or incorrect Share an idea

docs.title: Ask the community
docs.text:
• MeshCore Canada forum — searchable public discussions and support.
  • MeshCore Canada Discord — live community chat.

Include:

  • the device role and model;
  • the guide and step where you stopped;
  • what you expected;
  • what happened instead;
  • the Canada or local setting name, without secrets;
  • any error text after removing sensitive values.

docs.title: Stop before retrying when
docs.text:
• the next step would erase data you have not backed up;
  • the hardware is hot, damaged, wet, or wired unexpectedly;
  • you would lose the only way to reach a remote node;
  • a local operator says the proposed settings conflict with the mesh.

docs.title: Try one change at a time
docs.text: Return to Check your setup after making one change. Testing one change at a time makes the result easier to understand.

docs.title: Start with an observer
docs.text:
An observer listens through a MeshCore radio and sends network data to the live network viewer. Observing does not require repeating; a node can do both if configured for it. Observers can run on radio firmware, an always-on computer, or a home-automation host.

Read what the service collects and who can access it before enabling an observer.

Choose an observer setup

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Open the observer method chooser.
  • Pick a method that matches the radio, operating system, and host you already have.
  • Back up configuration before replacing firmware or installing a service.
  • Find your location code on the IATA region map. Use the same uppercase code in every broker entry; the nearest airport does not determine it.

docs.title: What setup changes
docs.text: Depending on the method, setup may replace radio firmware, install a host service, or add a home-automation integration. It also enables public network data publishing.

docs.title: Set up the observer
docs.text: Use the observer method chooser, then follow only the guide for the selected method.

docs.title: Use the right radio settings
docs.text:
The connected radio must use the same settings as the nearby mesh. Start with Canada and the 3-byte path setting unless your community lists different settings.

If Canada is not listed, follow the older-preset instructions.

Match your local mesh

Check the community directory. A connected observer can be online while hearing no useful traffic if its radio settings do not match nearby devices.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
The observer is working when:

  1. its radio hears known nearby mesh activity;
  2. it appears in the live observer list; and
  3. recent activity appears after a nearby transmission.

Use the observer verification checklist.

docs.title: Setup checklist
docs.text:
Checks are saved only in this browser.

  1. Read what observer data becomes public
  2. Choose a supported observer method
  3. Back up and prepare
  4. Follow the selected setup guide
  5. Apply local radio and service settings
  6. Check that the radio hears nearby activity
  7. Find the observer in the live network viewer

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Check the observer after radio, network, credential, host, or firmware changes. Open Check your observer for the detailed health view. If it is missing or quiet, get help.

docs.title: Start with a repeater
docs.text:
A repeater extends coverage by routing traffic for other users. Because it is fixed infrastructure, plan its power, antenna, access, and maintenance before installation.

Install and configure a repeater

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Check recommended repeater options.
  • Agree on the site and settings with the local community.
  • Keep physical recovery access while testing.
  • Record the current identity and settings before any erase or update.

docs.title: Know what flashing changes
docs.text: The guide installs repeater firmware and sets radio, identity, adverts, and regional settings. Test on the bench before a difficult installation.

docs.title: Flash the repeater
docs.text: Follow Flash and configure a repeater.

docs.title: Use the right radio and region settings
docs.text:
Use Canada with the 3-byte path setting unless your community lists different settings.

If Canada is not listed, follow the older-preset instructions.

Coordinate before installation

Check the community directory. Nearby repeaters need matching local settings, and operators should agree on changes that affect shared traffic.

Use the repeater configurator to select your MeshMapper IATA zone and independent scopes. Moving from the old region tree? Follow the migration steps before applying the new list.

Start with preparation. Keep working scopes in place and coordinate activation, including any edge blocking, with local operators.

JavaScript is required for the live duplicate-ID check. You can also [open the live node directory](https://live.meshcore.ca/?tab=Nodes).

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
The repeater is ready to install when:

  1. it keeps the intended settings after a reboot;
  2. it sends an advert; and
  3. a nearby known-good companion receives that advert.

Use the repeater verification checklist.

docs.title: Setup checklist
docs.text:
Checks are saved only in this browser.

  1. Confirm compatible hardware and site
  2. Back up and prepare
  3. Follow the flashing guide
  4. Apply local and regional settings
  5. Bench-check the repeater
  6. Test with a nearby companion

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Keep a record of the site, owner, recovery access, settings, and last successful check. Recheck it after firmware, antenna, power, or region changes. For firmware 1.14 or newer, review the coordinated loop-detection setting before changing a community repeater.

Review antenna and mounting guidance before final installation. If a check fails, get help.

docs.title: Start with a room server
docs.text:
A room server keeps a shared room available. It does not replace a repeater; use a repeater for routing and coverage.

Install and configure a room server

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Confirm the flasher offers room-server firmware for the device.
  • Decide who will maintain the room and retain recovery access.
  • Record any identity or settings you need before following an erase step.
  • Prepare separate guest and administrator credentials.

docs.title: Know what flashing changes
docs.text: The linked guide replaces the firmware and sets room-server identity, access credentials, and radio settings.

docs.title: Flash the room server
docs.text: Follow Flash and configure a room server. Use that guide for device selection, flashing, access setup, and recovery.

docs.title: Use the right radio settings
docs.text:
Use Canada with the 3-byte path setting unless your community lists different settings.

If Canada is not listed, follow the older-preset instructions.

Match your local mesh

Check the community directory. If your community publishes different settings, use those settings instead.

Keep administrator credentials private. Share only the guest access information intended for room users.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
The room server is ready when:

  1. a nearby companion discovers its advert;
  2. the companion can enter with the guest credentials; and
  3. the administrator can still recover and maintain it.

Use the room-server verification checklist.

docs.title: Setup checklist
docs.text:
Checks are saved only in this browser.

  1. Confirm compatible hardware
  2. Back up and prepare
  3. Follow the flashing guide
  4. Apply access and local settings
  5. Check the room server nearby
  6. Test discovery and guest access

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Record who maintains the room and how users get support. Ask a nearby community member to test it from a second companion. Recheck discovery and guest access after firmware, credential, or radio-setting changes. If discovery or access fails, get help.

docs.title: Check your setup
docs.text:
A powered-on device or a connected status does not mean setup is finished. Use the check for your device below.

Before testing, confirm the device still shows the Canada settings or your community's settings.

docs.title: Companion
docs.text:
1. Reboot after the last radio-setting change.
  2. Send an advert.
  3. Ask a nearby user with a known-good device to confirm that the advert appears.
  4. Exchange a test message when another user is available.

The companion is ready

A nearby known-good device sees the advert, and the two devices can exchange a test message.

If the advert is missing, compare radio and path settings before reflashing.

docs.title: Repeater
docs.text:
1. Keep the repeater accessible on the bench.
  2. Reboot it and confirm the intended settings remain.
  3. Send an advert from the repeater.
  4. Confirm a nearby known-good companion receives it.
  5. Repeat the check after any antenna, power, or installation change.

The repeater is ready

The repeater retains its settings and a nearby known-good companion receives its advert.

Keep it off hard-to-reach spots until the bench check passes.

docs.title: Room server
docs.text:
1. Reboot the room server.
  2. Send its advert.
  3. Confirm a nearby companion discovers it.
  4. Enter using the guest credentials.
  5. Confirm the administrator still has maintenance access.

The room server is ready

A companion discovers the room and guest access works without exposing the administrator credentials.

docs.title: Observer
docs.text:
1. Create nearby mesh activity with a known-good device.
  2. Confirm the observer radio is using matching settings.
  3. Open the live observer list.
  4. Find your observer and check for recent activity.
  5. Use Check your observer for the full health checklist.

The observer is working

Your observer appears in the live viewer and shows recent activity after a nearby transmission.

An online broker connection alone is not the final check.

docs.title: If a check fails
docs.text: If the check passes, you're done. If it does not, get help and describe what was missing.

docs.title: À propos de MeshCore Canada
docs.text:
MeshCore Canada est un projet communautaire destiné aux personnes qui utilisent MeshCore au Canada. Nous maintenons des guides de configuration, un répertoire des communautés, les données des régions canadiennes et des liens vers les outils partagés.

MeshCore Canada est indépendant du projet MeshCore officiel. Pour en savoir plus sur le micrologiciel, les applications et le protocole, consultez la documentation officielle de MeshCore.

docs.title: Ce que nous maintenons
docs.text:
• des guides de configuration, de matériel et de dépannage;
  • le répertoire des communautés canadiennes et la carte des régions;
  • des outils pour les répéteurs et les observateurs;
  • le code source du site Web.

Nous exploitons aussi des services MQTT et CoreScope partagés pour les utilisateurs canadiens. Ces services sont maintenus par Mr. Alderson, Ded, n30nex et Kranic.

docs.title: Participer
docs.text:

  • Obtenez de l’aide si une configuration ou une vérification du réseau échoue.
  • Partagez une idée ou signalez un problème.
  • Contribuez sur GitHub.

Ne publiez jamais de clés privées, de mots de passe, d’emplacements privés précis ni d’autres renseignements sensibles dans un formulaire, un billet GitHub, un forum ou une conversation.

Ne partagez aucun secret

docs.title: Soumissions publiques
docs.text:
Les idées et les propositions de limites deviennent des billets GitHub publics. Relisez l’aperçu avant de soumettre. N’incluez aucun mot de passe, aucune clé privée, aucune adresse résidentielle, aucune coordonnée privée ni aucun autre renseignement personnel.

Le service de soumission peut conserver des journaux de sécurité et de limitation du débit. Aucune période de conservation n’a encore été publiée.

docs.title: Données enregistrées sur votre appareil
docs.text:
Changer de langue ou passer entre la carte et le configurateur conserve votre sélection dans l’URL de destination. Elle peut contenir les coordonnées saisies, un lieu, des scopes de ville et de province et un profil radio. Ces URL peuvent apparaître dans l’historique du navigateur et les journaux du serveur. Ne partagez pas un lien qui contient un emplacement privé. Les résumés téléchargés omettent les coordonnées exactes et les identifiants de connexion.

Les listes de configuration, les brouillons d’idées et le dernier code de région Beacon choisi dans l’outil de vérification sont enregistrés uniquement dans votre navigateur lorsque vous utilisez ces fonctions. Les clés publiques des répéteurs, les mots de passe, les clés privées, les jetons antipourriel et les recherches d’emplacement n’y sont pas enregistrés.

Les totaux de l’en-tête sont mis en cache pendant cinq minutes dans l’onglet courant. La ville recherchée dans le répertoire apparaît dans l’URL pour partager ou retrouver les résultats.

Vous pouvez effacer les données enregistrées par ce site dans les paramètres de votre navigateur. Le formulaire d’idée offre aussi l’action Effacer le brouillon enregistré.

L’ancien éditeur de régions peut télécharger les brouillons conservés dans ce navigateur. Le téléchargement ne les envoie ni ne les supprime; ces brouillons ne sont pas des limites approuvées dans MeshMapper.
